title: Extensible Messaging and Presence Protocol (XMPP): Core
subtitle: How chat clients and servers open an XML stream, secure it, log in, and swap messages, presence and requests.
summary: XMPP Core defines how two programs, a client and a server or two servers, keep one long-lived TCP connection open and exchange small pieces of XML over it. It specifies how that stream is opened, encrypted with TLS, authenticated with SASL and tied to a particular device, and then defines three kinds of XML element (message, presence and iq) for chat, "who is online" and request-response. Instant-messaging behavior itself is left to RFC 6121. It obsoletes RFC 3920.

plainLanguage.summary: XMPP Core defines how a client and a server, or two servers, keep one long-lived TCP connection open and exchange small pieces of XML over it. It specifies how the stream is opened, encrypted with TLS and authenticated with SASL. It then defines three element types, message, presence and iq, for chat, availability and request-response. It obsoletes RFC 3920.

tldr.problem: Instant messaging in the late 1990s was a set of closed systems, and a chat protocol needed open, extensible, real-time messaging that works between independent servers.
tldr.mechanism: A client opens a TCP connection, both sides send an XML stream header, upgrade with STARTTLS, log in with SASL, bind a resource, and then send message, presence and iq stanzas down the same long-lived stream. Servers connect to each other the same way.
tldr.outcome: It gives a federated, XML-extensible messaging network in which anyone can run a server at their own domain, and it is still the base of deployed XMPP software. Note that stanzas are protected hop by hop, not end to end.

today: XMPP is still in everyday use. Server programs such as ejabberd, Prosody and Openfire implement it, and desktop and mobile chat clients speak it to those servers. RFC 7395 defines how to carry XMPP over WebSocket for browsers, and RFC 7590 later updated this RFC's guidance on using TLS. Many servers also support extensions published by the XMPP Standards Foundation, which sit outside this RFC.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Extensible Messaging and Presence Protocol (XMPP) is an application profile of the Extensible Markup Language (XML) for the near-real-time exchange of structured but extensible data between two or more network entities. This document defines the core: setting up and tearing down XML streams, channel encryption, authentication, error handling, and three communication primitives for messaging, network availability ("presence") and request-response.

The RFC explains that XMPP began in the Jabber open-source community, mainly in 1999, and that an IETF working group adapted it in the early 2000s. RFC 3920 and RFC 3921 were published in October 2004. This RFC incorporates experience gained since then and obsoletes RFC 3920. Address syntax moved to RFC 6122 and the instant-messaging and presence application to RFC 6121.

This RFC is the core transport and framing layer. It does not define what a "buddy list" or a "chat" is; that is RFC 6121.
sections.plainLanguage: XMPP (Extensible Messaging and Presence Protocol) is a way to exchange structured data in near real time using XML. This document defines the core: opening and closing XML streams, encryption, authentication, error handling, and three communication primitives. It began in the Jabber community and replaces RFC 3920.

sections.title: Architecture
sections.content:
Like email, XMPP uses globally unique addresses based on the Domain Name System. A server has an address like im.example.com, an account on it looks like juliet@im.example.com (a "bare JID"), and one connected device of that account looks like juliet@im.example.com/balcony (a "full JID"). "JID" stands for Jabber ID. The exact format is defined in RFC 6122.

XMPP also builds in presence, a way for an entity to announce that it is available, and persistent streams: each connection is a long-lived pair of XML streams rather than one request per connection, so data can be pushed at any time.

In practice the network is clients and servers talking to each other, and a server only talks to another server if its own policy allows. End-to-end the conversation is logically peer-to-peer, but physically it travels client to server to server to client.
sections.plainLanguage: XMPP addresses are based on DNS, like email. An account looks like juliet@im.example.com, and one connected device looks like juliet@im.example.com/balcony. Each connection is a long-lived pair of XML streams, so data can be pushed at any time, and presence lets an entity announce that it is available.

sections.title: Connecting over TCP
sections.content:
This RFC defines only one binding, to TCP. Before it can open a stream, the initiating side must find the receiving side's IP address and port. The preferred way is a DNS SRV lookup using the service name xmpp-client for client-to-server connections or xmpp-server for server-to-server connections, protocol tcp, and the domain, for example _xmpp-client._tcp.example.net.. The answer lists hosts and ports with priorities and weights, and the initiator tries them in order.

If the DNS gives no SRV answer at all, the initiator falls back to ordinary A or AAAA lookups on the domain and uses the default ports: 5222 for clients and 5269 for servers. If an SRV answer exists but no connection works, the RFC says the initiator should not fall back, to avoid a mismatch between inbound and outbound connections. A single SRV record whose target is "." means the service is deliberately not available at that domain.

The RFC also describes reconnection: a client that loses its connection should reconnect with a randomized delay rather than all at once.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC defines XMPP over TCP only. The initiating side first finds the receiver's address with a DNS SRV lookup, using the service name xmpp-client or xmpp-server. If DNS returns no SRV answer, it falls back to the domain's A or AAAA records and the default ports, 5222 for clients and 5269 for servers.

sections.title: XML streams and negotiation
sections.content:
An XML stream is a container for XML sent in one direction; a connection carries two of them, one each way. The initiating entity opens by sending a <stream:stream> header carrying to, optionally from, version='1.0', xml:lang, the content namespace (jabber:client or jabber:server) and the stream namespace http://etherx.jabber.org/streams. The receiver answers with its own header, which adds an id.

When version is at least 1.0, the receiver then sends a <stream:features/> element announcing what must or can be done next, such as STARTTLS, SASL mechanisms or resource binding. After each step that changes the security or identity of the stream (TLS and SASL), both sides restart the stream by sending fresh headers, because the old state no longer applies.

Order
Typically STARTTLS first, then SASL, then resource binding; the server advertises each only when it is time.
Closing
Each side ends with </stream:stream>; the RFC specifies the closing handshake in more detail than RFC 3920 did.
sections.plainLanguage: Each side of a connection sends its own XML stream. The initiator opens with a stream header naming the target domain, and the receiver answers with its own header. The receiver then announces stream features, such as STARTTLS or SASL mechanisms. After TLS or SASL succeeds, both sides restart the stream.

sections.title: TLS, SASL and resource binding
sections.content:
STARTTLS. If the server offers <starttls xmlns='urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:xmpp-tls'/>, possibly with <required/>, the client sends <starttls/>, the server answers <proceed/> or <failure/>, and the TLS handshake runs on the same TCP connection. On success the client opens a new stream.

SASL. The server lists mechanisms in <mechanisms/>. The client picks one with <auth mechanism='…'/>, the two exchange <challenge/> and <response/> elements carrying base-64 data, and the server ends with <success/> or <failure/>. The RFC defines eleven SASL error conditions such as not-authorized and account-disabled. After success, the stream is restarted again.

Resource binding. Finally the client sends an iq of type set containing <bind/>, optionally proposing a resource such as balcony, and the server replies with the full JID, for example juliet@im.example.com/balcony. The server may assign a different resource. If the requested name is already in use, the server may override it with a generated one (the encouraged behavior), refuse the bind with a conflict error, or end the older session. Only after binding does the client have a full JID for talking to other entities.
sections.plainLanguage: Negotiation has three steps. STARTTLS upgrades the same TCP connection to encryption with TLS. SASL (a standard authentication framework) then proves the client's identity through a challenge and response exchange. Finally, resource binding ties the stream to a particular device of the account.

sections.title: XML stanzas
sections.content:
After negotiation, a stream carries stanzas, the unit of meaning in XMPP. There are exactly three kinds. A <message/> is a "push": one entity sends data to another without expecting a reply. A <presence/> is a broadcast or publish-subscribe mechanism: a client normally sends it with no to and the server forwards it to everyone subscribed. An <iq/> (Info/Query) is request-response, similar in spirit to HTTP: types get and set are requests, and the answer is result or error with the same id.

All three share the attributes to, from, id, type and xml:lang. The server sets or checks from on client streams so that a client cannot forge its address. What goes inside a stanza is an extension payload in its own XML namespace, which is how XMPP stays extensible.

If a stanza cannot be processed, the entity returns the stanza kind with type='error' and an <error/> child of one of five types (auth, cancel, continue, modify, wait) plus one of 22 defined conditions, such as item-not-found or service-unavailable.
sections.plainLanguage: Once the stream is set up, it carries stanzas, of which there are three kinds. A <message/> pushes data to another entity without expecting a reply. A <presence/> is broadcast to subscribers. An <iq/> is a request that gets a result or an error.

sections.title: Stream errors and routing
sections.content:
Stream errors are different from stanza errors. A stream error means the whole stream is broken, for example badly formed XML, a wrong namespace or a policy violation. The RFC says stream errors are unrecoverable: the entity sends a <stream:error/> containing one of 25 defined conditions, closes the stream and drops the TCP connection. Examples include not-well-formed, host-unknown, conflict and see-other-host, which can redirect a client to another host.

For silent peers, the RFC separates a dead TCP connection, a broken stream and an idle peer. A single space character between stanzas is a permitted "whitespace keepalive", although not during TLS or SASL negotiation.

Section 10 gives server rules for processing stanzas, including in-order processing and what to do with a missing to address. A stanza for a remote domain goes over a server-to-server stream, which is opened the same way as a client one, with jabber:server as the content namespace.
sections.plainLanguage: A stream error means the whole stream is broken, for example badly formed XML or a policy violation. Stream errors are unrecoverable: the entity sends a <stream:error/>, closes the stream and drops the TCP connection. This differs from a stanza error, which affects a single stanza.

sections.title: Security considerations
sections.content:
The RFC covers security only for a single hop: client to server, or server to server. It states plainly that a stanza between two users on different servers crosses three streams, is handled as cleartext inside both servers, and that XMPP then has no end-to-end encryption technology to point to; that was left out of scope.

Clients and servers MUST support TLS. The mandatory-to-implement authentication is SASL SCRAM, specifically SCRAM-SHA-1 and SCRAM-SHA-1-PLUS, the latter with channel binding to the TLS session and preferred. This replaced DIGEST-MD5 as the required password-based method. For confidentiality the mandatory ciphersuite is TLS_RSA_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA. TLS plus SASL PLAIN is something clients should implement for interoperability but treat as a last resort. Implementations MUST support "strong security", meaning mutual authentication and integrity checking.

The cipher suite and TLS version in this 2011 text are dated; RFC 7590 updates the TLS requirements, so read the updating RFCs before deploying.

The RFC also describes certificate rules for server identity, DNS-related risks and presence leaks.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC covers security for a single hop only, from client to server or server to server. A message between users on different servers crosses three streams and is readable inside both servers. Clients and servers must support TLS, and the required authentication is SASL SCRAM.

items.title: TLS is mandatory to support
items.text: Clients and servers MUST implement TLS, negotiated in the stream with STARTTLS.

items.title: SCRAM for passwords
items.text: SCRAM-SHA-1 and SCRAM-SHA-1-PLUS are mandatory to implement; the PLUS variant adds channel binding and is preferred.

items.title: PLAIN only over TLS
items.text: Clients should implement it for interoperability but treat it as a last resort, and MUST NOT use it without TLS protection.

items.title: Hop by hop only
items.text: Protection covers one stream; servers see stanzas in the clear and end-to-end encryption is out of scope.
